newsitem.title: CHINA: China metal exchange reflects market fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: China metal exchange reflects market fundamentals.

text.p: China's fledgling Shanghai Metals Exchange (SHME) is beginning to offer a clear picture of the local market, reflecting its own growing maturity and that of Chinese metal producers, traders and industry experts said.
But the exchange, established just five years ago, still has a long way to go before giving a truly transparent picture of China's market, the experts polled in recent days said.

But in emulating the London Metal Exchange (LME), it is already performing the three major functions of a credible exchange: a price discovery mechanism, a hedging tool for producers, and a market that metal could be delivered to and from, experts in China, Hong Kong, Singapore and London said.
The SHME's most important copper contract is more and more a reflection of local market fundamentals, they said.

In the past few trading days, copper futures prices have plunged -- on Wednesday to their limit-down -- as Chinese producers raced to lock in prices before further anticipated falls, a futures trader with a major Chinese producer said.
Wednesday's volume, at 111,055 tonnes, was more than double that of the day before and contracts across the board lost between 640 yuan ($77) and 710 yuan ($85) per tonne.

Robin Bhar, head of research at LME broking firm Brandeis, said this was an indication that Chinese producers were using the exchange as a hedging tool, something that was being encouraged at the highest levels of the industry.
"At the end of the day, it's a global market, so copper prices, no matter where they are traded, should be influenced by the global fundamentals," Bhar said by telephone from London.
A perceived over-supply of copper in the Chinese market was the reason for flat and falling physical prices, he and other industry sources said.
And without any fresh market-making news, the SHME is expected to faultlessly follow the lead of the LME.

Prices on the LME have been falling this week, buckling under technical pressure and retreating from recent highs above $2,600 per tonne. Last three months business in Wednesday afternoon trading was $2,373, down $64 from Tuesday.

With the traditional summer slowdown weighing on the market, more falls were on the way, traders said. China's copper oversupply would compound the local falls, and the ongoing hedging activity, on the SHME.
The SHME is now the world's third biggest metal exchange although it still remains well behind the LME, where around 95 percent of the world's metals contracts are traded, and New York's COMEX.
Volumes remain relatively small, but at recent events to celebrate its fifth anniversary, local and international industry figures offered praise for its development so far.
Some sources pointed to moves by China's regulatory authorities to crack down on speculation in the futures markets.

"With the crackdown on speculation, you would have to think that the increase in volume and activity (on the SHME) indicates an increase in producer hedging," Bhar said, adding, "That's good for the market."
Some industry sources, however, said said they still did not consider movements in the exchange as a serious indicator of the market, noting that the LME made the market.
One analyst derided the exchange for the tiny volumes traded and the tiny volumes released as SHME warehouse stocks.
"It's just a small part of the whole picture and what is the point of that when you don't know how big the rest of the picture really is," he said.
China treats stocks of most commodities as a state secret and will not reveal how much copper the country has. Statistics that are made public are treated with skepticism.
-- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
